Welcome
'm very pleased to announce
that this month sees the start
of a new blog from the
Cheshire Clay Studio. Jacqui
Atkin and I first visited them in 2018,
when they were the Cheshire Clay
Collective, and we spent a lovely day
marvelling at the facilities they had.
Located on a farmyard, they had
inherited a huge glasshouse at the back of
the studio, which was perfect for 'outdoor'
firing, while still being under cover. The
team kept in touch with us, and we
learned that they'd been able to expand
their interior space to fill the rest of the
building.
Theirs is an interesting story of a
group coming together when the class
they were attending, closed. Keen to keep
everyone close, instead of finding an
alternative class, they decided to set up a
studio that they could all use. That was
just the start of what has grown into a
thriving business. Learning about the
challenges they face, and how they deal
with them, will make for very interesting
reading.
I live in Sussex, where it hasn't rained
for months and a hosepipe ban is about to
come into force. Electricity charges are
both ridiculous and very worrying, food

Summer learning at the Camborne
Contemporary Crafts Hub
Create CIC is developing a new contemporary crafts
hub for Cornwall, specialising in ceramics, glass and
jewellery. The hub provides community learning
facilities, with access to kilns and other equipment,
workshops, courses, and one-to-one specialist
tuition, whether you are just starting out on your
pottery journey or are an experienced ceramicist.
There is a wonderful mix of ceramics, glass and
jewellery courses and classes coming up. The
ceramics courses include a one-day class to make
your own macramé hanger and planter, which you
will construct and decorate using hand-building
techniques and slip decoration. There is also a
hand-building session where you'll make a sushi set
-chopstick rest, sushi platter, rice dish and dipping
bowl - using slab, press mould, coiling and pinching.
Six-week courses run throughout the year at
beginner and intermediate levels, with sessions
including exploring sagger firing, slip decoration,
colouring clay, large-scale creative coiling, large-
scale slab building, and porcelain, including paper
porcelain and lights.
Founder director Jane Smith is an artist working
in ceramics and glass. She says: "It is so important
for me to have a working life immersed in pottery
so I know the effect it can have on other people.
There's a reason why clay is used so often in
therapy - there is something so liberating about
clay, which gives you that connection with the
earth and allows creative exploration without being
precious. If you're not happy with what you have
made you can squidge it up and start again! It is so
easy to work collectively in clay - allowing people
to build something together that has real presence."

Before you begin:
A note about sponge shapes
Shaped sponges are widely available from craft
outlets or discount stores (in children's toy
departments) for very little cost. They are a little
difficult to cut to shape yourself, but you can
overcome the problem if you dampen it first and
then freeze it - a sharp craft knife should then easily
slice through the foam to create your chosen shape
Note about throwing: these torms are basically

to make many times throughout our 66 issues
of ClayCraft. The method for making both forms is
the same, so we are only showing the drainer here,
which has some added detail
A reminder when throwing -
to save wordy repetition!
Always compress the clay at the rim after each lift
- pinch the rim gently between your fingers and
thumb, at the same time resting the forefinger of
your other hand on the rim and applying gentle
pressure

Prepare the clay by kneading it well to remove any
possible trapped air.
You can work directly on the wheel head if you're
confident about lifting the drainer off when you've
finished - and we give you a tip to ensure you can
do this successfully - but otherwise, fix a batt to
the wheel head. You can find instructions on how to
throw a pad for a batt in issue 65 if you don't have a
quick-fix mechanism.
Centre 700g (1 ½lb) clay by forming the mass into
a rough cone shape, then position it at the centre of
the clean and dry wheel head.
Dribble a little water over the surface of the clay,
then pat it down to ensure it's secure.
Change the position of your hands to apply equal

up into a cone shape.
Flatten the cone down again, reverting your
hand position so the left is held firmly at one side
while the palm of your right hand pushes the clay
to centre with your fingers over the top to level the
mass.

GLAZE BASICS: RAW GLAZING
With the recent increase in energy costs,
many potters are looking for ways to reduce the
amount of energy they use for firing. One way to

be thick, like a slip. It also needs to be
high in clay so that it shrinks with the

crack and flake off. Raw glazes can
contain as much as 30% clay, or a

are preferable as they also supply silica

adding a solution of gum in water or a

and stirring thoroughly. When brushing
on a glaze, less water is absorbed into
the pot, so it is less likely to become too

used as a dipping glaze. Two or three

per hour up to 600°C, then up to 150°C
per hour for the rest of the firing. It is
really important that the pots are dry
before ramping up the temperature;
otherwise, they may explode. A preheat
for several hours at 80°C will ensure
everything is completely dry. A soak at
top temperature of 15-30 minutes will
help even out the temperature

FERMENTING FOOD
A fermentation crock works by creating the
conditions needed for the natural anaerobic
bacteria in the food to break down the sugars. The
result is an acidic environment, which prevents
rotting. It relies on maintaining an airtight seal for
fermentation to take place. The food is placed in
the crock, weighed down and the pot is topped off
with the pickling liquid. The lid is put on and water
is poured in between the crock's ring and the
cover to form an airtight seal.
This seal keeps out oxygen and contaminants,
allowing the anaerobic bacteria to thrive. The
bacteria break down lactose in the food to
produce lactic acid, giving the familiar 'tang'
associated with fermented food. Carbon dioxide
is produced by the breakdown of lactose. The
bubbles will rise to the surface and the gas
collects in the top of the lid, from where it must be
released every day.
With the rise in popularity of this ancient
preserving method, there are plenty of recipes to
be found online.
Korean Kimchi is Chinese cabbage leaves that
are rubbed in salt, rinsed, then fermented with
garlic, ginger, shrimp paste, sugar, gochugaru (red
pepper powder), spring onions and mooli (Daikon,
or white radish).
Sauerkraut uses very finely sliced cabbage,
which is salted to release its juices. The liquid is
kept to make the brining solution, and the cabbage
is tossed in black peppercorns and caraway seeds
before being added to the crock. It is covered with
its own brine and left to ferment.
Crocks can also be used to make kefir,
kombucha and pickles.

IMPORTANT -
Read before you begin:
In issue 65, we showed you how to plot and draw a
mandala design on paper, then transfer it to a leather-
hard plate that had been coloured in a single shade
of underglaze. If you need some inspiration, there are
some example patterns at the end.
This time, the same principles of preparation apply,
except the design is transferred to a raw leather hard
plate (without underglaze colour), and the outline of
the design is scored onto the surface using a pin for
clean, sharp lines rather than a sgraffito tool.
Begin by making your plate - it can be thrown in the
traditional way or made by the throwing hack we also
showed you in the last issue. You can make one from
a mould, use the foam-pressed method or one of the
methods we demonstrated in Issue 36, 'Easy Plate
formers'. Whichever method you choose, allow the
plate to firm to leather hard once made.
The example shown here was moulded using the
bisque plate ring we made in issue 40.
Measure the internal diameter of the plate and cut
out a template to that size, then plot out and draw
your design.
Place the template on the plate and transfer the
outline by drawing over the lines again to impress
them into the clay beneath.
Score the design into the clay using a pin held on its
side as far as possible, to avoid creating messy burrs.
If your plate has a rim like the one shown here, you
can continue the design over this once the centre
has been completed. Use flexible protractors or card
shapes and rulers to add the extra detail along with
small impressed stamp detail.
Allow the plate to dry out completely, then bisque
fire.
You will need:
• Bisque-fired, line-decorated plate
• Underglaze colours in as many shades as required,
including black or another dark, bold colour
• Brushes for application
• Cleaning cloth
• Transparent glaze (optional)

responsibly. WEAR A

Completely cover the
surface of the plate in
black underglaze or
a bold dark colour of
choice.
Really work the
underglaze into the
impressed detail with a
brush.
Allow the surface to
dry to the touch before
